questions.q: What does `np.arange(0, 1, 0.1).shape` return, and why is `arange` risky for float ranges?
options: `(10,)`, and `arange` is always exact for floats
`(10,)`, but rounding in the step can add or drop an endpoint for other float ranges
questions.why: `arange` excludes the stop and computes the length as `ceil((stop - start) / step)`. With floats that division can land just above or below an integer, so the count can be off by one. `np.linspace` with an explicit count avoids this.

questions.q: You need 5 evenly spaced points from 0 to 1 **including both ends**. Which call gives `[0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1]`?
questions.why: `linspace(start, stop, num)` includes the stop by default and spaces `num` points evenly. `arange(0, 1, 0.25)` stops before 1, giving only 4 points.

questions.q: What is the dtype of `np.array([1, 2, 3.0])`?
options: `float64`, since one float upcasts the whole array
questions.why: NumPy picks one dtype that can hold every element. A single float makes the array `float64`; mixing numbers doesn't produce an object array.

questions.q: `a = np.zeros((2, 3)); b = np.zeros_like(a, dtype=int)`. What are `b.shape` and `b.dtype`?
questions.why: `zeros_like` copies the shape and, by default, the dtype, but an explicit `dtype` argument overrides the dtype while keeping the shape.

questions.q: You pad ragged token lists `[[5, 2], [7], [1, 4, 9]]` into a `(3, 3)` array filled with `-1`. What is the second row?
questions.why: Right-padding keeps the tokens at the start and fills the rest with the pad value. Left-padding would give `[-1, -1, 7]`; filling with zeros would confuse padding with a real token id 0.

questions.q: Two calls to `np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=3)` are made in a row (a new generator each time). What do they return?
options: Different numbers, because the global state advances
The same numbers only if `np.random.seed(0)` was also called
The same three numbers both times
questions.why: Each call builds a fresh `Generator` from the same seed, so it starts in the same state. Calling `.normal` twice on **one** generator would give different numbers.

questions.q: An image of shape `(4, 4)` is cut into non-overlapping `2 × 2` patches with `img.reshape(2, 2, 2, 2).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(4, 4)`. What does each output row hold?
options: One flattened `2 × 2` patch, in row-major patch order
Every fourth pixel of the image
One column of the original image
One row of the original image
questions.why: The first reshape splits rows and columns into (block, offset) pairs; the transpose brings the two block indices together and the two offsets together, so the last reshape flattens each patch into a row.

questions.q: Which call creates a `(3, 3)` array whose border is 1 and interior is 0?
questions.why: Setting the interior slice to zero leaves a ring of ones. `np.pad(np.ones((1, 1)), 1)` does the opposite: a 1 in the centre surrounded by zeros.

questions.q: `a = np.arange(10); b = a[2:5]; b[0] = 99`. What is `a[2]` afterwards?
options: It raises an error: slices are read-only
`99` only if `a` is a float array
`99`, because basic slicing returns a view
questions.why: Basic slices share memory with the original array, so writing through `b` changes `a`. Use `.copy()` when you need independence.

questions.q: `a = np.arange(10); b = a[[2, 3, 4]]; b[0] = 99`. What is `a[2]` afterwards?
options: `2`, because fancy indexing returns a copy
`99`, because it is the same elements as `a[2:5]`
`99`, because integer arrays index by reference
questions.why: Indexing with an integer array (fancy indexing) always produces a new array. Only basic slices and views like `reshape` share memory.

questions.q: `x = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)`. What is `x[:, 1::2]`?
questions.why: All rows, columns starting at 1 with step 2: columns 1 and 3.

questions.q: You add gradients into an embedding table with `G[ids] += g` where `ids = [3, 3, 1]`. What goes wrong?
options: Row 3 receives only one of its two updates; use `np.add.at(G, ids, g)`
It raises an error for repeated indices
questions.why: `G[ids] += g` is a read, add, write on a fancy-indexed copy, so for a repeated index the last write wins. `np.add.at` performs unbuffered accumulation.

questions.q: `x = np.array([3, -1, 4, -2])`. What is `x[x > 0]` and its shape?
questions.why: Boolean masking keeps the selected elements and returns a 1-D copy. `np.where(x > 0)` or `np.flatnonzero` would give the indices.

questions.q: For BERT-style masking you set `inputs[mask] = MASK_ID` and want the labels to keep the original ids. Which ordering is correct?
questions.why: `labels = inputs` and `inputs[:]` both alias the same buffer, so masking inputs would also overwrite the labels. Only an explicit copy preserves the originals.

questions.q: `x` has shape `(5, 3)`. What is the shape of `x[:, None, :]`?
questions.why: `None` (alias `np.newaxis`) inserts a length-1 axis at that position, here between the two existing axes.

questions.q: To take a centre crop of size `h × w` from an image `(H, W)`, which start row is right when `H - h` is odd?
options: `(H - h) // 2`, which puts the extra pixel at the bottom
questions.why: Slicing needs integers; floor division gives a consistent rule. `(H - h) / 2` is a float and raises an `IndexError` in NumPy.

questions.q: Which pair of shapes broadcasts?
questions.why: Shapes are aligned from the right; each dimension pair must be equal or contain a 1. `(4, 1)` with `(3,)` becomes `(4, 1)` with `(1, 3)`, which broadcasts to `(4, 3)`.

questions.q: `X` is `(n, d)`. You compute `X - X.mean(axis=1)`. What happens?
options: It subtracts each row's mean from that row
It always works because NumPy aligns by name
It fails for `n ≠ d`; row means need `keepdims=True` or `[:, None]`
questions.why: `X.mean(axis=1)` has shape `(n,)`, which aligns with the **last** axis of length `d`. Unless `n == d` (where it silently does the wrong thing) it fails. Keep the reduced axis so it broadcasts over columns.

questions.q: For a pairwise Manhattan distance matrix between `A` `(m, d)` and `B` `(n, d)`, which expression is correct?
questions.why: Inserting axes gives `(m, 1, d)` and `(1, n, d)`, which broadcast to `(m, n, d)`; summing the last axis gives `(m, n)`. The memory cost is $m\cdot n\cdot d$.

questions.q: You min-max scale each column of `X` with `(X - X.min(0)) / (X.max(0) - X.min(0))`. One column is constant. What do you get in that column?
questions.why: Float division by zero in NumPy produces `nan` or `inf` with a warning instead of raising. A common guard is `np.where(rng == 0, 1, rng)`.

questions.q: Standardising a test set, which statistics should you use?
options: No statistics; standardise each test row by its own values
The test set's own mean and std
The training set's mean and std
The mean and std of train and test combined
questions.why: Using test statistics leaks information about the test distribution and makes train and test features inconsistent. Fit on train, apply everywhere.

questions.q: `counts` is `(n, k)`. Which line turns each row into a probability distribution?
questions.why: Row sums with `keepdims` have shape `(n, 1)` and broadcast across columns. Without `keepdims` the `(n,)` vector aligns with the columns instead.

questions.q: `a` has shape `(3, 1)` and `b` has shape `(1, 4)`. How many elements does `a * b` have?
questions.why: Both length-1 axes are stretched: the result is `(3, 4)`, the outer product.

questions.q: Pairs of item prices whose sum is within a budget: `p[:, None] + p[None, :] <= budget`. What shape is the boolean result for `p` of length `n`?
options: `(n, n)`, including each item paired with itself on the diagonal
questions.why: Broadcasting builds the full matrix, diagonal included. Take `np.triu(..., k=1)` or the indices with `i < j` to keep each unordered pair once.

questions.q: Which is the fastest correct way to compute $\sum_i x_i^2$ for a large float array?
options: `for v in x: total += v * v`
questions.why: `x @ x` runs a single compiled BLAS loop. The other options run a Python-level loop over every element.

questions.q: Cyclical encoding of hour of day uses $(\sin(2\pi h/24), \cos(2\pi h/24))$. Why both?
options: Two features always train faster than one
The cosine adds a bias term
Each alone maps two different hours to the same value; together they are unique
The sine is undefined at midnight
questions.why: $\sin$ takes each value twice per cycle (for example hours 3 and 9), so a single feature is ambiguous; the pair places the hours on a circle, keeping 23 and 0 close.

questions.q: What does `np.argsort(np.argsort(x))` give for `x = [30, 10, 20]`?
questions.why: The first `argsort` gives the order `[1, 2, 0]`; the second inverts that permutation, giving each element's rank. Ties need extra handling (averaged ranks) because this breaks them by position.

questions.q: For a normalised difference index $(a - b)/(a + b)$ on arrays with some $a + b = 0$, which is safest?
options: `np.divide(a - b, a + b, out=np.zeros_like(a, dtype=float), where=(a + b) != 0)`
`(a - b) / (a + b)` and ignore the warning
questions.why: `np.where` still evaluates the division everywhere and emits warnings (the bad values are only discarded afterwards). `np.divide` with `where=` skips those entries entirely and leaves the `out` value.

questions.q: RMSNorm computes `x / np.sqrt((x ** 2).mean(-1, keepdims=True) + eps)`. What does it **not** do that LayerNorm does?
questions.why: RMSNorm only rescales by the root mean square; LayerNorm also centres each row. Dropping the mean saves a reduction and works as well in practice for LLMs.

questions.q: `np.percentile(x, 50)` and `np.median(x)` for `x = [1, 2, 3, 4]` return what?
questions.why: With the default linear interpolation, the 50th percentile of an even-length array is the mean of the two middle values, the same as the median.

questions.q: A loop computes `y[i] = x[i] - x[i - 1]` for `i ≥ 1`. Which vectorized form matches it?
questions.why: `np.diff` gives length `n - 1` differences. `x - np.roll(x, 1)` also wraps the first element around against the last, which the loop never computes.

questions.q: `a.sum(axis=0)` on a `(3, 4)` array returns what shape?
questions.why: The reduced axis disappears: summing over axis 0 collapses the 3 rows, leaving one total per column.

questions.q: `np.nanmax([[1, np.nan], [np.nan, np.nan]], axis=1)` returns what?
options: `[1, nan]` with a warning for the all-NaN row
questions.why: `nanmax` ignores NaNs, but an all-NaN slice has no value to return, so it gives NaN and emits a `RuntimeWarning`. Handle that case explicitly if it matters.

questions.q: Winsorizing a column at the 5th and 95th percentiles does what?
options: Clips values to those percentile values
Rescales the column to the range `[0.05, 0.95]`
questions.why: Winsorizing keeps every row and caps extreme values, which `np.clip(x, lo, hi)` does once the two percentiles are known.

questions.q: Splitting a 1-D signal of length 10 into frames of length 4 with hop 2 gives how many full frames?
questions.why: Frame starts are 0, 2, 4, 6; a frame at 8 would need samples 8 to 11. The count is $\lfloor(10 - 4)/2\rfloor + 1 = 4$.

questions.q: Which function produces overlapping windows of an array without copying data?
questions.why: `sliding_window_view` returns a view with adjusted strides, so each window shares memory with the original. `np.split` makes non-overlapping pieces.

questions.q: To remove a weekly seasonality from daily data you take `x[7:] - x[:-7]`. What length is the result for $n$ days?
questions.why: Seasonal differencing at lag 7 pairs each day with the same weekday a week earlier, losing the first 7 days.

questions.q: `np.correlate(a, b, mode='full')` for lengths $n$ and $m$ has how many entries?
questions.why: Full mode evaluates every relative shift where the two signals overlap by at least one sample. Finding the peak index and subtracting $m - 1$ gives the lag.

questions.q: What does `np.clip(x, 0, None)` do?
options: Removes negative values from the array
Sets negative values to 0 and leaves the rest
Raises an error, because both bounds are required
questions.why: `None` means no bound on that side, so this is equivalent to `np.maximum(x, 0)` (a ReLU). The array keeps its shape.

questions.q: `np.unique([3, 1, 3, 2], return_counts=True)` returns what?
questions.why: `np.unique` returns the sorted unique values; with `return_counts` it also returns how often each occurs. Use `return_index` and sort by it if you need first-seen order.
